# Interpretation and further questions {#sec-discussion}

The analysis establishes a sharp division of responsibilities.  All frozen Metropolis kernels target the same \(\pi\), so their common invariant distribution determines the deterministic Oja mean field.  A&M's Markov theory controls the failure of successive observations to be independent.  The polar retraction preserves orthogonality while contributing only an absolutely summable second-order error.  The target mean--covariance energy controls noncompact coordinates, and the PCA energy identifies the eventual subspace equilibria.

The result should not be read as an assertion that online Oja necessarily selects the leading \(r\)-dimensional eigenspace.  Its limiting stationary set contains **every invariant \(r\)-subspace** of \(C\), including non-leading eigenspaces.  Deterministically, the leading subspace is locally attracting under an eigengap, whereas non-leading invariant subspaces have unstable directions; showing that Markov-driven stochastic iterates almost surely avoid unstable equilibria requires additional hypotheses on noise excitation and is a distinct problem.  The Lyapunov literature of @plumbley1995 is relevant to that refinement.

There is also an important distinction between two possible algorithms.  We have analyzed a *sample-driven* Oja increment, using \((X_{n+1}-\mu_n)(X_{n+1}-\mu_n)^\top\).  Its mean-field perturbation from the target Oja flow depends on \((\mu-m)(\mu-m)^\top\).  If one instead updates \(W\) using the *estimated covariance* \(\Gamma_n\), then \(\dot W=(I-WW^\top)\Gamma W\), with a different coupling error depending on \(\Gamma-C\).  The same composite Lyapunov method can treat this variant, but the stochastic innovation and Poisson step must be stated consistently with the chosen update.

Finally, the localized result does not settle the probability-one finite-reinitialization question for the **enlarged** algorithm.  Under the concrete Gaussian random-walk kernel, the necessary kernel bounds are available from A&M, and the new coordinate is compact.  Establishing the exact manifold-compatible stability theorem, with the reinitialization map and boundary conditions stated, is the remaining step before claiming unconditional convergence of the original adaptive procedure.  This is recorded transparently in the internal proof audit.

The present theorem is therefore a useful foundation for investigating principal-subspace adaptation with Markov rather than independent innovations.  It identifies the precise non-i.i.d. bookkeeping, proves a localized limiting-subspace result, and leaves the stronger global stability and leading-eigenspace selection questions clearly separated.
